clue.text: Isn't Mrs T. Hardy a model for a novel?

indicators.note: to model clay is to shape it, so these letters are reshaped into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these words, used just as written, are the raw material

explanation.surface: A reader wonders whether Thomas Hardy's wife inspired some character in fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole run of letters up to 'a' is the fodder; 'model' looks like part of the question about inspiration but is the anagram signal. Tristram Shandy is Laurence Sterne's eighteenth-century comic novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterne's rambling comic work of fiction, The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, is a famous English book of that kind.

clue.text: Trio aim to pass part of driving test

parts.note: a trio is a group of three
to aim a weapon is to point it
to pass into a state is to turn into it, as milk turns sour

explanation.surface: Three people aim to get through a section of their driving exam.
explanation.definitionFit: The manoeuvre of reversing a car round in a narrow road in three movements is a standard driving examination task.

clue.text: Popular papers ask for information

parts.note: something in fashion is said to be in
a quire is a set of 24 or 25 sheets of paper

explanation.surface: Tabloid newspapers go asking questions to dig up a story.
explanation.definitionFit: To inquire is to put a question so as to learn something, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Tess tries to change the unhappy state of France

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made to change their order

parts.note: the two words supply their own letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: Hardy's heroine Tess sets out to cure a nation's gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of France' flags that the answer is a French word, borrowed into English.
explanation.definitionFit: Tristesse is the French word for sadness or melancholy, used in English for a wistful mood.

clue.text: A twerp and a hooligan getting worked up

parts.note: taken as written
a git is a British insult for a foolish or contemptible person
taken as written
a Ted, short for Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth often seen as a troublemaker

explanation.surface: A fool and a thug are both losing their tempers.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone worked up is anxious or excited, which is the state of being agitated.

clue.text: Still sad, yet restless

indicators.note: letters that are restless will not stay in place, so they move about

parts.note: the two words supply their own letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is unmoving and gloomy, yet cannot settle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' sits beside 'restless' as an apparent contradiction; it is the definition, as an adjective meaning not moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Steady means firm and unmoving, the same as keeping still.

clue.text: Rocky road to ecstasy and love

indicators.note: a rocky road is shaken up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word supplies its own letters, taken as written
E is the street name for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A hard path leads on to bliss and romance.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore someone is to love them deeply; the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Determined to be late to class

parts.note: the late so-and-so is someone who has died
a set is a group of pupils taught together

explanation.surface: A pupil is set on arriving late for a lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dead set on something means being firmly resolved to do it.

clue.text: Uncomfortable feeling in legs and hands

parts.note: pins is informal for legs
taken as written
the hands of a dial or gauge are its needles

explanation.surface: A tingling discomfort in the limbs, of the sort that follows sitting awkwardly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names the prickling sensation felt as circulation returns to a numb limb.

clue.text: Compulsory Scripture class is quite unusual

parts.note: RE is religious education, the school subject once called Scripture

indicators.note: an unusual version of the words has their letters out of the usual order

parts.note: the two words supply their own letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A school's mandatory Bible lesson turns out to be rather odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Something requisite is required or necessary, much as a compulsory item must be done.

clue.text: Old fellow originally interpreted for Arab

parts.note: a fellow is a man

indicators.note: originally points to the start of the word interpreted

parts.note: only its opening letter is used

explanation.surface: An elderly man once acted as translator for an Arab.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Oman, on the Arabian Peninsula, is an Arab by nationality.

clue.text: Not the first un-PC person to walk the earth!

indicators.note: the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: someone who discriminates by sex is politically incorrect

explanation.surface: A jibe that bigots have been around since the dawn of humanity.
explanation.definitionFit: To exist is to be alive and present in the world, as living creatures that walk the earth are.

clue.text: Talks to father about clothes

indicators.note: about signals that the word for father turns round

parts.note: da is an informal name for a father
to clothe someone is to dress them

explanation.surface: A parent lectures about what to wear.
explanation.definitionFit: To address someone is to speak to them directly, a synonym of the verb phrase.

clue.text: Has a management position abroad, we hear

indicators.note: the word for abroad is spoken and the answer shares its sound

parts.note: to be abroad is to be in a foreign land beyond the sea

explanation.surface: Someone is a manager in a foreign posting, so rumour has it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who oversees others supervises them, which is the job of a manager.

clue.text: Rod's working in Lancashire town

parts.note: a bolt is a metal rod or bar used to fasten a door
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A man named Rod has a job in a northern English town.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod looks like a man's name; here it is a metal bar. Bolton is a town near Manchester, historically in Lancashire, a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolton is a large former mill town in north-west England, traditionally part of the county.

clue.text: Tom's abroad, following tortuous route extremely far away

indicators.note: Tom's letters come after those of route
a tortuous route twists about, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word supplies its own letters, taken as written

indicators.note: abroad also means astray or out of place, so these letters are scattered

parts.note: the name and its S supply their own letters

explanation.surface: Tom is overseas after taking a winding road to somewhere remote.
explanation.definitionFit: The outermost point is the one farthest from the centre, the most remote.

clue.text: Hits iffy, unorthodox half-century or so

indicators.note: the letters depart from their normal order

parts.note: the two words supply their own letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A batsman scrapes about fifty runs with some dubious strokes.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a half-century is fifty runs by one batsman, which suits the surface; here it means an age of about fifty years.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiftyish means about fifty, typically in age, the number a half-century counts.

clue.text: Horrible gunge finally set in lump

indicators.note: the horrible gunge is mangled into a different order

parts.note: the word supplies its own letters, taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word set

parts.note: only its closing letter is used

explanation.surface: Revolting sludge eventually hardens into a solid blob.
explanation.walkthrough: Gunge is British slang for a sticky, messy substance.
explanation.definitionFit: A nugget is a small rough piece of something, especially gold, so a small lump.

clue.text: Surly genius making face

parts.note: a surly, forbidding look is grim
an ace is an expert, someone brilliant at something

explanation.surface: A grumpy prodigy is pulling an expression.
explanation.walkthrough: Face is a noun here, the twisted expression someone makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a contorted facial expression, the face one pulls in pain or disgust.

clue.text: Sporting event, one taking place in Bath and part of London

indicators.note: the letter for one is set within the city's name

parts.note: taken as written
the first three letters of the city's name

explanation.surface: A competition is being staged in two English cities.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a Georgian spa city in the west of England. The biathlon combines cross-country skiing and rifle shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: The biathlon is a two-discipline winter contest of skiing and shooting, an Olympic event.

clue.text: Abandoned any old doctrine for socialist principles

parts.note: something abandoned has been left behind
an ism is any distinctive belief or theory

explanation.surface: Someone dropped a tired creed in favour of left-wing ideals.
explanation.definitionFit: Leftism is the politics of the left, the body of socialist ideas and beliefs.

clue.text: A desire to be accepted

parts.note: taken as written
greed is an excessive desire for more

explanation.surface: Someone longs to be welcomed into the group.
explanation.definitionFit: Something agreed has been consented to by those involved, so it is accepted.

clue.text: Dog's happy it's at the back of car

definitions.text: it's at the back of car

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely, to tail them
a light heart is a happy one

explanation.surface: A pet is pleased to be riding in the rear of the vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog' reads as the animal; it is a verb meaning follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A rear lamp on a vehicle, glowing red to warn traffic behind, sits at the rear of a vehicle.

clue.text: Girl has one cold drink

parts.note: lass is a northern British and Scottish word for a girl

explanation.surface: A young woman is enjoying something chilled.
explanation.definitionFit: A lassi is a chilled yogurt beverage from South Asia, often sweet or salted.

clue.text: Lifer contrived to get weapon

indicators.note: contrived means put together artfully, so these letters are reassembled

parts.note: the word supplies its own letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A long-term prisoner managed to get hold of a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a long-barrelled firearm, one kind of weapon.

clue.text: Gathers fresh pears

indicators.note: a fresh version is newly made, with the letters in a new order

parts.note: the word supplies its own letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone picks newly ripened fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: To reap is to harvest a crop, so it means gathering it in.

clue.text: Real idiot misread article

indicators.note: misreading the words jumbles their letters

parts.note: the two words supply their own letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A genuine fool got a newspaper piece wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial is a newspaper piece giving the paper's own opinion, a kind of article.

clue.text: Bum with newspaper and old hat

parts.note: bum is British slang for the buttocks, a behind
The Times is a London daily newspaper

explanation.surface: A rear end paired with a daily paper and a worn-out hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Old hat is an idiom for outdated, not a piece of headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: Being outdated or old-fashioned is to have fallen out of step with modern ways.
